title: Scaling Compute on Context — Jack Morris, Engram
talk_summary: Jack Morris of Engram frames 'scaling compute on context' as the problem of teaching a pre-trained model a private, unstructured corpus D when data scaling and from-scratch training are off the table, leaving compute as the only axis. He surveys naive continued training, KV/context compaction, on-policy distillation, synthetic continued pre-training, and unsupervised RL, arguing all saturate on a fixed dataset and that self-improvement (progressively harder self-generated training) is the missing ingredient.

takeaways.technique: Compaction as a bounded, lossy shortcut
takeaways.what_they_do: Compress long context into a small set of KVs so the model behaves as if the data were in context, but notes it only covers what fits and loses gradient-based learning.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you take this really long context, which is D, and then you try to compress it into some set of KVs

takeaways.technique: Synthetic Q&A distillation from a private corpus
takeaways.what_they_do: Generate question/answer pairs conditioned on the private data and train the model to answer as if it had seen the source in context (self-study / cartridges-style).
takeaways.evidence_quote: generate like question and answer pairs conditioned on D and then train the model to behave as if it is seeing D in context

takeaways.technique: Watch for saturation, then escalate difficulty
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues any fixed dataset eventually saturates ('data wall'), so the useful signal is whether added compute keeps improving; they look for curves that keep rising via self-generated harder data.
takeaways.evidence_quote: eventually you will fit the data and you'll know some about D, but you won't know everything

takeaways.what_they_do: Describes recursively generating data, getting a slightly better model, then generating better/harder data, as the mechanism behind AlphaGo-style gains, versus one-shot distillation that plateaus.
takeaways.evidence_quote: AlphaGo makes its own training questions harder by getting better through training
